mcqs.question: Calling .map(f) on None instead of Some(5) — what happens to f?
options: f is called with None passed directly as its argument
f is called with a default placeholder value substituted for the missing one
map throws an exception because there's nothing to apply f to
f is never called at all, and the result is simply None
mcqs.explanation: map only applies its function when there's a value present; on an empty box it short-circuits and returns the same empty box without ever invoking the function. There's no substitution, no exception, and the function is never given None as an argument.

mcqs.question: Why can't plain map alone combine two independent Option<int> values with a two-argument add function?
options: map can only be called once per program, so a second call is disallowed
map's function argument takes one plain value, so applying a two-argument function through map leaves you with a box holding a function still waiting for its second argument
add is not a pure function, so map refuses to accept it
Option types cannot hold functions, only plain values
mcqs.explanation: map is built for one-argument functions applied to one boxed value; feeding it a two-argument function produces a partially-applied function still wrapped in a box, not a final combined result — that gap is exactly what applicative closes. The other options misstate real constraints; add is pure and boxes can hold functions.

mcqs.question: Using map (not flatMap) to apply find_manager — which itself returns an Option<Manager> — to a Some(user), what shape does the result have?
options: A flat Option<Manager>, identical to what flatMap would produce
An Option<Option<Manager>> — a box nested inside a box, since map doesn't flatten a box-returning function's result
A plain Manager value with no wrapping at all
None, regardless of whether find_manager succeeds
mcqs.explanation: map wraps whatever the function returns in the outer box without flattening, so a function that itself returns Option<Manager> produces Option<Option<Manager>> — a box inside a box. flatMap exists specifically to collapse that extra layer, which is why it's needed instead of map here.

mcqs.question: Compared to a nested-if chain checking for None at every step, what changes when the same logic is written as a flatMap chain?
options: The short-circuiting behavior changes — flatMap runs every step regardless of earlier failures
flatMap chains require converting every value to a list first
The short-circuiting behavior is identical; only the shape of the code changes — no growing indentation, and each step's None-check is handled once inside flatMap itself
flatMap chains are only usable with numeric types, not arbitrary objects
mcqs.explanation: Both versions stop at the first None with identical results; flatMap doesn't change the semantics, it removes the need to repeat the same manual guard at every nesting level, keeping the code flat instead of growing a pyramid of indentation. It has no list requirement and works on arbitrary boxed types, not just numbers.

mcqs.question: In JavaScript, why does chaining .then(fn) where fn itself returns a Promise not produce a Promise<Promise<T>>?
options: Because .then is exactly a flatMap operation — it auto-flattens a Promise returned by fn instead of nesting it
Because JavaScript Promises cannot be nested under any circumstances
Because .then only accepts functions that return plain values, never Promises
Because async/await must be used instead whenever fn returns a Promise
mcqs.explanation: .then behaves as flatMap: when the callback returns a Promise, .then automatically flattens it into the chain rather than nesting it, which is exactly the monadic behavior described earlier in this topic. .then does accept callbacks that return Promises — that's the common case — and async/await is optional sugar over the same mechanism, not a requirement.

mcqs.question: An interviewer asks you to explain a monad. Which opening is the stronger answer, according to this topic?
options: Reciting the category-theory definition first, then working backward to an example if there's time
Declining to answer since monads are too abstract to explain briefly
Listing every language that has monads without explaining the underlying mechanism
Starting with a concrete box like Optional, walking through map's limitation, then introducing flatMap as the fix — naming 'monad' only at the end
mcqs.explanation: Building the concept up from a concrete example and only naming it at the end demonstrates real understanding, which is what interviewers are checking for — starting from jargon is the tell that often signals memorization without comprehension. Declining to answer or just listing languages doesn't demonstrate understanding either.
